column2: How is the fast prescribed then? Tell, O son of Suta. Sauti said: "When, O Brahmins, nothing of the earlier one is found on Dvadashi,
then the day of the sun, moon and... is the supreme day to fast. Among Brahmins disputing in the conflicts of many scriptures,
the holy Dvadashi is to be fasted, and the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth. When the Ekadashi is spoiled and the Shravana star arrives,
the holy Dvadashi is to be fasted in both fortnights. This decision has been told to you by me from the decision of the scriptures.
If you wish to hear anything else, tell me." The sages said: "Tell the rule of the Yugadi days properly and as they are, Sauti.
For you nothing is unknown, even of the sun's transits and the like." Sauti said: "The wise know two bright and two dark Yugadi days:
in the bright half the forenoon is to be taken; in the dark half the afternoon. The solstice is rich in parts of the day; the transit is sixteen palas.
When the earlier one has passed in the south, the north is held; at the equinox in the middle time it is declared imperishable.
Having known the tithi, O Brahmins, as stated by the year-reckoner, the fast must be kept; otherwise one goes to hell.
A man who observes the one joined with the earlier cuts away his dharma, for the destruction of offspring and the loss of prosperity.
Even at a pala's contact, O best of Brahmins, one should avoid the auspicious (eleventh) joined with the tenth, as one avoids Ganga water touched by a drop of liquor.
The five cow-products touched by a dog, spoiled by the tenth — one should avoid; the Ekadashi in both fortnights, O best of Brahmins.
That tithi joined with the earlier was given long ago by Yadu-crested Vishnu to the demons, O best of Brahmins, for the pleasing of the great-souled.
Wealth given at the wrong time, to unworthy recipients, O best of Brahmins, what is given by the enraged, what is given without respect,
what is given on a tithi joined with the earlier is given to demons; what is given with leavings, what is given to the fallen,
what is given to those conquered by women, what is given without water, what is given with boasting — that is given to demons.
Therefore, O Brahmins, an Ekadashi tithi spoiled should not be kept, as the husband of a Shudra woman destroys merit and shraddha.
What is given, chanted, offered, bathed or worshipped to Hari on a spoiled tithi perishes, as darkness at sunrise.
As women, proud of youth and tormented by Love, abandon an old husband, so the wise abandon contact with another tithi, always for the increase of dharma.
Narada said: "No cry is heard, O king, in the courtyard of the hells, and no ledger is written of the doers of evil deeds.
This Chitragupta stands silent like a sage; why do the sinners not come to your house?
They are overcome by deceit and pride and devoted to wicked deeds." Thus addressed by the great Narada,
the king, son of Vivasvan, said with some dejection. Yama said: "Narada, this king now on the earth,
devotee of Hrishikesha, the ancient Supreme Person, the lord of kings, awakens the people with a drum:
'One must not eat, one must not eat when Hari's day arrives. Whatever mortals eat, they go to my punishments.'
Through fear of that all people keep the Dvadashi. Even by pretext, O best of sages, fasting on Dvadashi,
they go to the Vaishnava world free of burning or dissolution. By serving Dvadashi people go to Hari's abode.
By that king, O best of Brahmins, my roads are blocked now; the hells are made empty and so are the worlds of the gods.
The scribes' writings are weary; they are written and wiped away by the people through the power of the Ekadashi fast, O best of Brahmins.
People, even with sins like Brahmin-slaying, by fasting without eating on Vishnu's day go to Hari's abode.
So I have become, O great sage, like a deer in a forest fire, like a twice-born man without eyes, ears, or twilight rites,
or like a man conquered by women, an impotent man, or the lord of women. I, giving up desire, having such lordship of a guardian of the world,
shall go to Brahma's world to make my sorrow known. An official who is idle and stays in his appointed post
eats his master's wealth and surely goes to hell." Sauti said: "Having said this, Yama, O Brahmins, with Narada
went to Brahma's abode with Chitragupta. He saw him seated, surrounded by beings with and without form,
the support of the Vedas, seed of the world, great-grandfather of all, the self-born, abode of beings, called Om, stainless,
pure, abode of purity, the swan, Brahma, marked by kusha grass, served by various guardians of the world and lords of the directions,
with epics and Puranas and the Vedas standing with the planets, by the embodied oceans, rivers and lakes,
by embodied trees, especially the ashvattha and others, by wells, lakes and ponds, and embodied mountains,
by days and nights, fortnights, months and years, O Brahmins, by kalas, kashthas and winks, by seasons, courses and ages,
by Manvantaras, kalpas, moments, winks, by stars, yogas, karanas, the full moon and the new moon,
by pleasure and pain, pairs of opposites, gain and loss, victory and defeat, truth and falsehood, the Lord of gods, the fire of dharma, encircled,
served by men skilled in action and others, Pitamaha with sattva, rajas and tamas,
the Lord with natural modifications peaceful, deluded and fierce, with wind, phlegm and bile embodied as named diseases,
the Soul of the universe, resting in the supreme dharma by bliss, himself maker of the world, surrounded by beings too unnamed,
served by embodied abuse, harsh words and the like. Among them the son of the Sun entered, bashful like a bride.
Looking downward, with bowed face he showed himself. Seeing Yama, with Narada, come in person,
they said to each other with wide eyes: 'Why is this the sun's son here? He has come to see the maker of the worlds, god Pitamaha.
This son of the sun is always busy, without a moment free; why has he come, to ask the welfare of the gods?
I think it is a very great wonder that the scribe has come with a wiped cloth (ledger) in great dejection.
The ledger of this righteous man was wiped by no one; what was never seen or heard is seen here.'
While those beings spoke so, the son of the Sun, who had been given his instruction, fell before Brahma, O Brahmins,
like a tree cut at the root, crying 'Save, save!': 'I am disgraced, O Lord of the gods, that my ledger has been wiped.
I see myself bereft though you are my lord, O Lotus-seated.' Saying so, O best of Brahmins, he became motionless.
Then a cry arose in the assembly: 'This one who makes all beings, moving and unmoving, weep —
why does this Yama, son of Vivasvan, weep in pain? Or this saying seems to us a worldly truth:
one who causes pain to people soon suffers himself; the doer of evil deeds never gets anything good.'
Then the Wind stopped their speech, knowing the opinion of the people of equal minds, and of Brahma.
Driving off the doubt, the Lord, the world-embodied noble-minded one, slowly lifted Mercury-like Yama with his well-formed arms.
He seated the agitated one, who was fleeing, on a seat, and said to the sky-formed son of the sun, who was with his body:
'By whom have you been overcome? By whom driven from your place? By whom was your divine ledger, the ledger of the world, wiped?
Tell all without remainder, Kushaketu (Yama) here speaking. He who is lord of all, dear one, will raise you up; he will remove the sorrow in your heart, O son of the sun.'
Thus addressed by the Wind, the son of the Sun then spoke, looking at the face of Brahma, son of Kushaketu, in a choked, soft voice:

Abandoning all dharmas, abandoning ancestor-worship, abandoning worship of gods, and bathing in holy places and the like, even women,
naradapuran:128:12	abandoning both yoga and Sankhya, knowledge and the knowable, honourable one, abandoning study and offerings, and having done many sins,
naradapuran:128:13	men go to the Vaishnava world by fasting on Hari's day, together with their ancestors and grandfathers;
naradapuran:128:14	their fathers' fathers also, and the mother's-side grandfathers who are the mother's father and the rest;
naradapuran:128:15	and their parents' ancestors. This sorrow again, O God, pierces my vitals:
naradapuran:128:16	the beloved's fathers go, having wiped away my writing; since from the fathers' seed, since she held in her womb,
naradapuran:128:17	what one does alone, he alone enjoys; hence what is done by another, O Brahma, the seed born from the mother...
naradapuran:128:18	saves both sides, in whose body there is the body of the ancestor. A wife is not the seed, nor the womb-bearer;
naradapuran:128:19	how, O Lord of the world, does her side go to the highest state? By the power of the son-in-law's merit my head aches.
naradapuran:128:20	I have no use, O God, for such an appointment. He who fasts on Ekadashi leaves me and goes to Hari,
naradapuran:128:21	uplifting three families together with himself, O lotus-born; leaving my path he goes to Hari's abode.
naradapuran:128:22	A man does not obtain such a goal by sacrifices, O God, nor by holy places, gifts or vows without Vishnu.
naradapuran:128:23	Dying in water or fire, he does not obtain that goal, nor lost in yoga or by a fall from a precipice, O Ordainer;
naradapuran:128:24	he does not go to such a state as the Vaishnava-vow-keeper does, O best of the wise: this is truly said.
naradapuran:128:25	On Hari's day a man anointed with (rice) from the Creator's fruit, free of desire and eating moderately, goes to the world of the Earth-bearer, though of evil deeds and born a man.
naradapuran:128:26	I, hopeless, deficient in deeds on earth, have come to your pair of lotus feet. Make, for the cause of creation and preservation, the time of my petition the time of fearlessness.
naradapuran:128:27	Then sinners lacking (their fate), the men by my bound-with-chains-and-ropes attendants, would come near me and fall under my power.
naradapuran:128:28	The road broken, heated by the sun, that Vishnu's hosts with very strong hands, having freed the hell-pot, all the throng of people go to that abode of the Supreme.

Fasting on Vishnu's day, they go to his world by the king's command. He is our great enemy, especially yours.
naradapuran:129:5	He must be restrained, O Lord of the world; there is no doubt. By him the earth was ruled a thousand years,
naradapuran:129:6	and an innumerable people were taken to Hari's Vaishnava world, placed on Garuda, made four-armed,
naradapuran:129:7	clothed in yellow, garlanded, fair-eyed. If he, dear to Madhava, stays in Madhava's month, O Lord of gods,
naradapuran:129:8	he will take the whole world to Vishnu's faultless abode. This is the staff, this the ledger, released by your feet.
naradapuran:129:9	The incomparable guardianship of the world, wiped away by that king Rukmangada, O Lord of gods — blessed is she who bore him.
naradapuran:129:10	Born of the mother for the destruction of all sorrow, superior in qualities; what use is a son who troubles his mother?
naradapuran:129:11	One who does not scorch enemies like the sun in the month of Jyeshtha — in vain does his mother have labour pains, a bad mother of a bad son, O God.
naradapuran:129:12	He whose fame does not flash like lightning in a cloud, who does not uplift his father's side by learning or by strength,
naradapuran:129:13	is a disease of his mother's womb born on earth. A son who is hostile to dharma, wealth and desire
naradapuran:129:14	is called a mother-killer by the good; his life is in vain. A woman who bears a hero is rare, O Brahma, without doubt,
naradapuran:129:15	she by whom Rukmangada was born, for the wiping away of Malli. This was not established on earth by any king, O God;
naradapuran:129:16	in the Purana too, O Lord of the world, wiping away of the ledger has not been heard of. I do not know, ever, seeing the Lord of the Milk Ocean stand in Hari's service, sounding a dreadful drum, stopping my road.
Our Lord of the world, the Supreme Person who gives birth — how can fools rule one who serves his day?
You were not crushed by them, you were not bound firmly by them; our respect has been shown; you do not understand the truth.
An official who does not know the best royal devotees on earth, who is full of toil, is restrained by them in turn.
The king's favourites should not be employed by an official when they are at fault; accomplished by their master's favour, they would harm the official.
Thus those who bow to Janardana though sinners — how are they to be restrained by you, O son of the Sun, from childhood?
By Shaivas or devotees of the Sun, or my devotees, or Hari's devotees, I do help you, but not against devotees of Hari or the Sun.
Of all the gods the first is the Supreme Person.
Restraint of devotees of Madhusudana is not possible. By those who have kept Dvadashi in both fortnights even by pretext,

when they are insulted, I am not your helper. If I help you, O son of the Sun, injustice that destroys my body would occur to me, a fall from Brahma's state, as if from the holiest, if I act against Vishnu's devotees."
As you were created by me in mind, fair-hued one, so you have become, O fair-limbed, maddening of the mind.
She then bowed to the four-faced one and said: "Look, O Lord, the moving and unmoving world is swooning,
bewildered by my form, even the stainless yogi. There is no man in the three worlds who, on seeing me,
beginning with you, O lotus-born, does not fall into agitation. One wishing good should not praise himself.
By self-praise even a pure man goes to hell. Yet praise should be made, O Brahma, for the sake of a purpose.
I, created by you, O Brahma, am for agitating someone. Command me, Lord of the world, whom I shall agitate, without doubt.
Even a mountain on earth is bewildered on seeing me, O God; what then of a man with consciousness who breathes in and out?
So too in the Puranas the description of a woman's glance is said to madden men and destroy hard vows.

'A man stays on the right path, his senses prevail, he has shame and keeps humility, only so long as the arrows of the glances of playful women, with arched-bow brows reaching the ear, blue lashes, do not fall and steal firmness from his heart.'
Cursed is the poetry of a foolish bad poet who equates a woman's face with the moon; where in the moon are glances of astonishment at a brow's play, anger, favour and smiles?
Wine drunk by a man bewilders even the wise; but a young woman remembered or seen bewilders a man more than liquor.
You created me, great-grandfather, for bewildering men; command me, Lord of the world, I shall bewilder the three worlds."
Brahma said: "You speak truly, goddess; nothing is impossible in the three worlds, O fair-hipped, elephant-gaited one.
You who disturb even my mind, O fair-hued one — that I have grasped well and subdued with the goad of knowledge.
How will you not steal the minds of the worlds? This is true, large-eyed: your form is bewildering.
I see the entire world with its gods inactive. For what purpose I created you, accomplish that, fair-faced one.
In the city of Vidisha on earth is a king named Rukmangada, whose wife Sandhyavali is like you in form, auspicious one.
Of her was born a son Dharmangada, greater than his father, with the strength of ten elephants, with splendour like the sun.
In patience equal to the earth, in depth like the ocean, in energy blazing like fire, in anger like Yama,
in giving like Bali, in speed like the wind, in gentleness equal to the moon, handsome like Love,
in policy equal to Jupiter and Venus, that prince; by his father the whole of Jambudvipa was enjoyed, fair-faced one.
By Dharmangada other continents were also conquered; out of shame to his parents he did not know the pleasure of women;
thousands of wives who came of themselves were abandoned by him; he does not stray from his father's word, staying in his father's house,
who has three hundred mothers, O lovely-smiling gold-bright one, and sees them all alike.
Go, fair-limbed, to that king devoted chiefly to dharma, adorned with a jewel of a son, on the best of mountains, Mandara.
There the king will stay, carried far by his horse; bewildered by your singing, fair-limbed, he will leave the horse, amazed.
Climbing the mountain's back he will come to meet you. There, goddess, you must say, after meeting the king:
'I shall be your wife, O king, without doubt; what I say, Lord, you must surely do.'
Bewildered by your form, he will agree so; then, making him take oaths with his right hand,
after a few days have passed you must say to him, fair-browed one: when you see him infatuated in love-play,
then, laughing, you should remind the king of his earlier word: 'The oath you made, O king, in keeping my word —
keep that, O king; I regard it as a pact.' When you have said so, the king, bewildered but through respect for truth,
will say: 'I shall keep it, without doubt; tell me what I shall give you.' When he has said so, you must say, fair-faced one:
'King Rukmangada, father of Dharmangada, auspicious one, you must never keep the fast on Hari's day.
Let the fast for me be one of love-play, dear.' One who does not serve his own very tender, youthful wife,
devoted to parva-days, of bad conduct, surely goes to hell. 'For three nights I have been cast off by you, O king, because of fasting;
I cannot stay even a moment without you. At the time of shraddha, when Brahmins are seated, if the wife asks for union,
she is then to be enjoyed.' Even when addressed thus, if the king will not do your word, fair-hued one, you must then say a further word:
'If, O king, you do not give up the fast on Hari's day, cut off the head of your son Dharmangada with your own fine sword
and throw it on my lap yourself, O king. If you do not do this which is dear to me, O king,
you, spent in dharma, will go to hell, without doubt.' Hearing your words, fair-bodied one, he will not kill his son, equal to his life;
taking the words of the Brahmins, he will enjoy on Madhava's day.
Then people will go to Yama as before, bound by the nooses of his servants; the dwelling in hell will be as much as the writing; you will have done well.
But if the king, truthful and glorious, slays his son, he will go to the abode of Padmanabha worshipped by all the gods."
When a great period of ten thousand years was passing, this bracelet-rubbing was done by the Discus-bearer's god.
This mountain is the abode of jewels, with many minerals.
The great mountain, the pleasure-ground of the denizens of heaven, the cause of the austerity of ascetics, increaser of the delight of celestial women, the source of jewels and herbs...
